summary: Updates the wildcard definition from RFC 1034. It changes how wildcards interact with CNAME, removes an error condition and rewrites the wording for some central concepts. The goal is to refine the definition, not to change how wildcards behave. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: A DNS wildcard is a record whose owner name starts with an asterisk label, and a server uses it to answer queries for names nobody wrote down. This RFC tightens the definition of when that happens, so that different servers behave the same way.

questions: what is a closest encloser in dns
how do wildcards work with cname records
subtitle: Precise rules for when a DNS wildcard answers a query, and how wildcards and CNAME records interact.

tldr.problem: The wildcard definition in RFC 1034 was incomplete and confusing, and implementations had drifted apart from it in different ways, which also tangled the design of DNSSEC authenticated denial.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines new terms (wildcard domain name, asterisk label, closest encloser, source of synthesis), restates what it means for a name to exist, and adds one rule so that a CNAME found at a wildcard is handled like an exact-match CNAME.
tldr.outcome: Wildcard behaviour is now described precisely enough for interoperability. Of all the changes, only the CNAME rule affects implementations, and the RFC updates RFC 1034 and RFC 2672.

facts.label: Terms defined
facts.value: Asterisk label, wildcard domain name, source of synthesis, closest encloser, label match

today: RFC 4592 is a Proposed Standard from July 2006. It updates RFC 1034 and RFC 2672, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What This RFC Changes
sections.content:
RFC 1034, sections 4.3.2 and 4.3.3, describe the synthesis of answers from special resource records called wildcards. That definition is incomplete and has proven to be confusing. This document describes the wildcard synthesis by adding to the discussion and making limited modifications. The modifications close inconsistencies that have led to interoperability issues, and the description does not expand the service intended by the original definition.

Many DNS implementations diverge, in different ways, from the original definition of wildcards. The impetus for the document was the engineering of the DNS security extensions: with an unclear definition of wildcards, the design of authenticated denial became entangled.

The document limits its changes, documenting only those deemed necessary based on implementation experience, and stays as close to the original document as possible. Relevant sections of RFC 1034 are repeated verbatim, each line beginning with a hash character, so that the old and new text can be compared. The document is focused on wildcards as defined in RFC 1034; nothing is implied about alternative means of synthesizing resource record sets.

It accomplishes three tasks: it defines new terms, makes minor changes to avoid conflicting concepts, and describes the actions of certain resource records as wildcards. The new terms are the asterisk label and the wildcard domain name, both in section 2.1.1, and the source of synthesis, closest encloser and label match, all in sections 3.3.1 and 3.2.
sections.plainLanguage: The original description of DNS wildcards was incomplete, and servers had each filled the gaps differently. The main worry was DNSSEC: when the rules for wildcards are unclear, it is hard to work out how to prove that a name does not exist. This RFC keeps the original behaviour and only fixes the parts that caused different servers to disagree.

sections.title: The Asterisk Label and Wildcard Domain Names
sections.content:
The syntax of a wildcard is the same as any other DNS resource record, across all classes and types. The only significant feature is the owner name. Because wildcards are encoded as resource records with special names, they are included in zone transfers and incremental zone transfers just as non-wildcard resource records are.

A wildcard domain name is defined by having its initial, that is leftmost or least significant, label be, in binary format, 0000 0001 0010 1010, which is 0x01 0x2a in hexadecimal. The first octet is the normal label type and length for a 1-octet-long label, and the second octet is the ASCII representation for the asterisk character. A descriptive name of a label equalling that value is an asterisk label. RFC 1034's definition of wildcard would then be a resource record owned by a wildcard domain name.

No label values other than that one are asterisk labels, so names beginning with other labels are never wildcard domain names. Labels such as the*, or a label made of two asterisks, are not asterisk labels and do not start wildcard domain names.

The RFC also removes the restriction in RFC 1034 section 4.3.3 that the domain part of a wildcard owner name should not contain other asterisk labels. The original documentation was incomplete and the restriction served no purpose given years of operational experience. A wildcard domain name can have subdomains, and there is no need to inspect them for another asterisk label. A wildcard domain name can also be an empty non-terminal, in which case any lookup encountering it terminates as would any empty non-terminal match.

When a wildcard domain name appears in a message's query section, no special processing occurs: an asterisk label in a query name only matches a single corresponding asterisk label in the existing zone tree when the RFC 1034 algorithm is being followed. When a wildcard domain name appears in the resource data of a record, no special processing occurs either; an asterisk label in that context literally means just an asterisk.
sections.plainLanguage: A wildcard is an ordinary DNS record whose owner name begins with a single label holding the asterisk character. Only that exact label counts: a label such as the* does not make a wildcard. This RFC also drops an old rule that stopped a wildcard name from containing a second asterisk, and says plainly that an asterisk in a query or in a record's data is just an ordinary character.

sections.title: When a Name Exists
sections.content:
The notion that a domain name exists is mentioned in the definition of wildcards, because RFC 1034 says wildcard records do not apply when the query name, or a name between the wildcard domain and the query name, is known to exist. The definition of what exists in RFC 1034 is unclear, so this RFC gives a new one.

RFC 1034's wording is fixed by the following paragraph: the domain name space is a tree structure. Nodes in the tree either own at least one RRSet and have descendants that collectively own at least one RRSet. A node may exist with no RRSets only if it has descendants that do, and this node is an empty non-terminal. A node with no descendants is a leaf node, and empty leaf nodes do not exist.

At a zone boundary the domain name owns data, including the NS RR set. In the delegating zone the NS RR set is not authoritative, but that is of no consequence here: the domain name owns data, and therefore it exists.

Empty non-terminals are domain names that own no resource records but have subdomains that do. The tree definition in RFC 1034 section 3.1 says that each node and leaf corresponds to a resource set, which may be empty, so empty non-terminals are explicitly recognised and they exist.
sections.plainLanguage: A name counts as existing when it holds data, or when something below it holds data. A name in between, holding nothing itself but sitting above real names, is called an empty non-terminal and still counts as existing. A name at the end of a branch with nothing below it does not exist. The reason this matters is that a wildcard only applies when nothing along the way already exists.

sections.title: The Example Zone and Its Answers
sections.content:
The RFC uses a small zone to show how wildcards apply. It holds *.example. with TXT and MX records, a name sub.*.example. with a TXT record, the names host1.example. and host2.example., SRV records under _ssh._tcp, and a delegation subdel.example..

Queries that are answered from a wildcard include host3.example. with QTYPE MX, which is answered from the wildcard's MX record, and foo.bar.example. with QTYPE TXT, which is answered because bar.example. does not exist but the wildcard does. A query for host3.example. with QTYPE A gets no error but no data, because there is no A RR set at *.example..

Queries that are not answered from a wildcard include host1.example. with QTYPE MX, because that name exists, and sub.*.example. with QTYPE MX, because that name exists too. A query for _telnet._tcp.host1.example. with QTYPE SRV is refused because _tcp.host1.example. exists even without data. A query for host.subdel.example. with QTYPE A is refused because subdel.example. exists and is a zone cut. A query for ghost.*.example. with QTYPE MX is refused because *.example. exists.

That last case highlights a common misconception: a wildcard blocks itself, in the sense that a wildcard does not match its own subdomains. *.example. does not match all names in the example. zone, because it fails to match the names below *.example.. To cover names under *.example., another wildcard domain name is needed, *.*.example., which covers all but its own subdomains.
sections.plainLanguage: Wildcards fill in names that are missing from a zone, but they stop as soon as they reach a name that exists. They also stop at themselves: *.example. does not cover names below *.example., so a second wildcard, *.*.example., is needed to reach further down.

sections.title: Closest Encloser, Source of Synthesis and the CNAME Rule
sections.content:
RFC 1034's algorithm for building a response has three parts in step 3. Part 'a' is an exact match that results in an answer, part 'b' is a referral, and part 'c' is the case where label matching runs into a label that does not exist, as if the lookup had fallen off the tree. Once one of the parts is chosen, the others are not considered, and label matching is done independently of the query type.

To describe part 'c', the RFC coins a term for the last node that was matched. The closest encloser is the node in the zone's tree of existing domain names that has the most labels matching the query name, counting consecutively from the root label downward. Each match is a label match, and the order of the labels is the same. The closest encloser is by definition an existing name, and it might be an empty non-terminal or a wildcard domain name. In no circumstances is the closest encloser used to synthesise records for the current query.

The source of synthesis is the wildcard domain name immediately descending from the closest encloser, provided that this wildcard domain name exists. Immediately descending means a name of the form <asterisk label>.<closest encloser>. A source of synthesis does not guarantee having an RRSet to use for synthesis, because it could be an empty non-terminal. If the source of synthesis does not exist, there is no wildcard synthesis, and there is no search for an alternate. For any given lookup there is at most one place at which wildcard synthetic records can be obtained.

The RFC then adds one rule. If the data at the source of synthesis is a CNAME and the query type does not match CNAME, the server copies the CNAME RR into the answer section, changes its owner name to the QNAME, changes the QNAME to the canonical name in the CNAME RR, and goes back to step 1. This is essentially the same text as part 'a', which covers the processing of CNAME RRSets found at an exact match.
sections.plainLanguage: When a lookup misses, the server works out how much of the query name does exist. That part is the closest encloser, and the only wildcard it will consider is the one directly below it, the source of synthesis. If that wildcard is not there, the answer is simply that the name does not exist. The one behaviour change is that a CNAME found at a wildcard now redirects the query in the same way as a CNAME found at an exact match.

sections.title: Wildcards and Special Record Types
sections.content:
Several record types get special treatment when they are the result of an exact match, and this section works out what that means when the same type sits at a wildcard domain name. The types covered are SOA, NS, CNAME, DNAME, SRV, DS, NSEC, RRSIG, and none, meaning an empty non-terminal wildcard domain name.

An SOA RRSet at a wildcard domain name means the domain is at the root of the zone. A zone apex cannot be a source of synthesis, because a source of synthesis is by definition a descendant of the closest encloser. There is still no reason to forbid a wildcard domain name from owning an SOA RRSet.

For an NS RRSet at a wildcard domain name the RFC gives no definition. The dilemma is a conflict between the synthesis rules in part 'c' and the fact that the resulting synthesis generates a record for which the zone is not authoritative, which in a DNSSEC signed zone makes signature management unclear. Prior to DNSSEC this appeared workable, and some deployments do it, but continuing to allow it is not tenable with DNSSEC because the synthesis is done in a zone that has delegated away responsibility for the name. Outright banning it is also untenable, since the DNS protocol does not define how to handle illegal data. A compromise that redefined wildcards of type NS as not being used in synthesis would have required significant edits to the DNSSEC signing and validation work. With no consensus forming, and with wildcards of type NS being a rarity in operations, the semantics are left undefined until there is a clear need, and including them in a zone is discouraged but not barred.

Ownership of a DNAME RRSet by a wildcard domain name is a threat to the coherency of the DNS and is to be avoided or outright rejected. Two caches fed different records from the same wildcard DNAME would rewrite queries differently and cease to be coherent. A wildcard DNAME could also synthesise a DNAME below a name that already owns a DNAME, which the DNAME definition forbids.

For SRV, the definition's use of the word Name is easily confused with the owner name. Once the _Service and _Proto labels are removed from the owner name of an SRV RRSet, what remains could be a wildcard domain name, but that is immaterial to the RRSet. For DS, a DS RRSet owned by a wildcard domain name is meaningless and harmless. For NSEC, synthesis happens only when the query exactly matches the record, and synthesised NSEC records are never used in negative caching or to generate a negative response. RRSIG records are synthesised along with the data, and the owner name being synthesised is not a problem because the label count in the RRSIG instructs the verifying code to ignore it. If a source of synthesis is an empty non-terminal, the response has no error in the return code and no RRSet in the answer section.
sections.plainLanguage: Some record types behave differently when they come from a wildcard instead of an exact match, and this section spells out each case. A wildcard should not hold a DNAME record, because different caches would then rewrite the same query in different ways. A wildcard holding an NS record has no defined meaning and is discouraged. Records of other types are either harmless or behave as they would at an exact match.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document refines the specifications to make it more likely that security can be added to DNS. No functional additions are made, just refining what is considered proper, to allow the DNS, the security of the DNS, and extending the DNS to be more predictable.
sections.plainLanguage: The point of tidying up the wildcard rules is to make DNSSEC possible. The RFC adds nothing new; it only makes the existing behaviour predictable enough to sign and validate.

data.title: Zone example.
data.code:
$ORIGIN example.
example.                 3600 IN  SOA   <SOA RDATA>
example.                 3600     NS    ns.example.com.
example.                 3600     NS    ns.example.net.
*.example.               3600     TXT   "this is a wildcard"
*.example.               3600     MX    10 host1.example.
sub.*.example.           3600     TXT   "this is not a wildcard"
host1.example.           3600     A     192.0.2.1
_ssh._tcp.host1.example. 3600     SRV   <SRV RDATA>
_ssh._tcp.host2.example. 3600     SRV   <SRV RDATA>
subdel.example.          3600     NS    ns.example.com.
subdel.example.          3600     NS    ns.example.net.

viz.caption: THE SAME ZONE AS A TREE OF NAMES
CLOSEST ENCLOSER AND SOURCE OF SYNTHESIS FOR EACH QUERY NAME
HOW EACH RECORD TYPE BEHAVES AT A WILDCARD DOMAIN NAME

items.title: SOA
items.text: Marks a zone apex. Can never be a source of synthesis, but a wildcard may still own one.

items.title: NS
items.text: No definition is given. Inclusion in a zone is discouraged, but not barred.

items.title: CNAME
items.text: Redirects the query like a CNAME found at an exact match. This is the one behaviour change.

items.title: DNAME
items.text: A threat to cache coherency. Avoid it or reject it outright.

items.title: SRV
items.text: The Name in the record definition is not the owner name, so a wildcard there is immaterial.

items.title: DS
items.text: Meaningless and harmless at a wildcard domain name.

items.title: NSEC
items.text: Synthesised only on an exact match, and never used for negative caching.

items.title: RRSIG
items.text: Synthesised with the data. The label count tells the verifier to ignore the owner name.
